On subsets of lattice cubes avoiding affine and spherical degeneracies

Anubhab Ghosal , Ritesh Goenka and Peter Keevash Address: Mathematical Institute
University of Oxford
Oxford, UK OX2 6GG Email address: {ghosal,goenka,keevash}@maths.ox.ac.uk
Abstract.

For integers 1<k<d−11<k<d-1 and r⩾k+2r\geqslant k+2, we establish new lower bounds on the maximum number of points in [n]d[n]^{d} such that no rr lie in a kk-dimensional affine (or linear) subspace. These bounds improve on earlier results of Sudakov-Tomon and Lefmann. Further, we provide a randomised construction for the no-four-on-a-circle problem posed by Erdős and Purdy, improving Thiele’s bound. We also consider the random construction in higher dimensions, and improve the bound of Suk and White for d⩾4d\geqslant 4. In each case, we apply the deletion method, using results from number theory and incidence geometry to solve the associated counting problems.

Key words and phrases: 
no-four-on-a-circle, no-three-in-line, evasive sets.
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
05D40, 52C10, 52C35

1. Introduction

At the beginning of the 2020th century, Dudeney [15] posed the following problem: How many points can be placed in an n×nn\times n integer grid so that no three points lie in a straight line? This is now well known as the no-three-in-line problem and has been extensively studied (see [9, Section 10.1] and [23, F4]). Several similar problems have been studied since then, namely, problems that seek to maximize the size of subsets of lattice cubes while avoiding specific configurations. Such problems are fundamental not only in discrete geometry but also relevant across other fields. For instance, higher dimensional finite field analogues of no-three-in-line sets provide examples of evasive sets [35] (see also [38]), which provide explicit constructions of list-decodable error correcting codes [22] and bipartite Ramsey graphs [35], and are also related to the cap set problem [13, 17] from extremal combinatorics. The no-three-in-line problem can also be viewed as a discrete analogue of Heilbronn’s triangle problem [23, F4] (see [11] for recent progress on the latter) from discrepancy theory, which asks for a placement of points in the unit square that maximizes the area of the smallest triangle.

Brass and Knauer [8] asked the following generalized problem: given n,d,k,r∈ℕn,d,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<dk<d and r⩾k+2r\geqslant k+2, what is the maximum number faff​(n,d,k,r)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r) of points in [n]d[n]^{d} such that no rr of these points lie on a kk-dimensional affine subspace? The case r=k+2r=k+2 [9, Section 10.1, Problem 5] is of special interest since it corresponds to sets that avoid up to kk-dimensional affine degeneracies. Further specializing to k=d−1k=d-1 [9, Section 10.1, Problem 3] is even more interesting since it corresponds to sets in general linear position. We will prove the following lower bound on faff​(n,d,k,r)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r).

Theorem 1.1.

Let d,k,r∈ℕd,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<dk<d and r⩾k+2r\geqslant k+2. Then faff​(n,d,k,r)=Ω⁡(fd,k,r​(n))f_{\mathrm{aff}}(n,d,k,r)=\Omega(f_{d,k,r}(n)), where

fd,k,r​(n)={nd⁡(1−k/(r−1)), if ​r⩽d,nd−k/(log⁡n)1/d, if ​r=d+1,nd−k, otherwise.f_{d,k,r}(n)=\begin{cases}n^{d(1-k/(r-1))},&\text{ if }r\leqslant d,\\ n^{d-k}/(\log n)^{1/d},&\text{ if }r=d+1,\\ n^{d-k},&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

In particular, if r=k+2r=k+2, then faff​(n,d,k,k+2)=Ω⁡(fd,k​(n))f_{\mathrm{aff}}(n,d,k,k+2)=\Omega(f_{d,k}(n)), where

fd,k​(n)={n/(log⁡n)1/d, if ​k=d−1,nd/(k+1), otherwise.f_{d,k}(n)=\begin{cases}n/(\log n)^{1/d},&\text{ if }k=d-1,\\ n^{d/(k+1)},&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

An obvious upper bound for faff​(n,d,k,r)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r) is (r−1)​nd−k(r-1)n^{d-k} as can be seen by partitioning [n]d[n]^{d} into nd−kn^{d-k} translates of [n]k×{0}d−k[n]^{k}\times\{0\}^{d-k}. Brass and Knauer [8, Section 2] noted that lower bounds matching up to a constant are known in some special cases:

  • •

    for k=1k=1 and r>dr>d, as can be seen by considering points on the modular moment surface x1+x22+⋯+xdd≡qmodpx_{1}+x_{2}^{2}+\dots+x_{d}^{d}\equiv q\mod p, and

  • •

    for k=d−1k=d-1, as can be seen by taking points on the modular moment curve {t↦(t,t2,…,td)modp}\{t\mapsto(t,t^{2},\dots,t^{d})\mod p\},

where pp is a prime between ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil and nn. A matching lower bound was also obtained by Pór and Wood [34] for the case d=3,k=1,r=3d=3,\,k=1,\,r=3 by taking a suitable positive density subset of points on the modular paraboloid {(x1,x2)↦(x1,x2,x12+x22)modp}\{(x_{1},x_{2})\mapsto(x_{1},x_{2},x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})\mod p\}. For 1<k<d−11<k<d-1, Brass and Knauer [8, Lemma 8] showed that for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an integer r⩾k+2r\geqslant k+2 such that faff​(n,d,k,r)=Ω⁡(nd−k−ε)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r)=\Omega(n^{d-k-\varepsilon}). More recently, Sudakov and Tomon [38, Theorem 1.4] improved this result by showing faff​(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(nd−k)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(n^{d-k}) for r>dkr>d^{k}. Theorem 1.1 implies faff​(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(nd−k)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(n^{d-k}) for r>d+1r>d+1, thereby improving upon Sudakov and Tomon’s result.

As noted above, algebraic constructions are known to yield improved lower bounds in some special cases. Similarly, taking lattice points on a strictly convex surface yields a lower bound of Ω⁡(nd−2+2/(d+1))\Omega(n^{d-2+2/(d+1)}) for no-three-in-line sets in [n]d[n]^{d} [6] (see also [16]). This is also the best possible bound that can be obtained using such a construction since the maximum number of points in [n]d[n]^{d} lying on a strictly convex surface is O⁡(nd−2+2/(d+1))O(n^{d-2+2/(d+1)}) by a result of Andrews [2]. This bound is better than the one in Theorem 1.1 for k=1, 3⩽r⩽d/2+1k=1,\,3\leqslant r\leqslant d/2+1. For the remaining subcases of k=1k=1, namely, d/2+1<r⩽dd/2+1<r\leqslant d, Lefmann [30] (see also [31]) showed that it is possible to improve the bound in Theorem 1.1 by a polylog factor using the results of Ajtai, Komlós, Pintz, Spencer and Szemerédi [1] on independent sets in hypergraphs. For all the remaining cases, namely, 1<k<d−11<k<d-1, Theorem 1.1 improves upon the previously best known bound of Ω⁡(nd−k−k⁡(d+1)/(r−1))\Omega(n^{d-k-k(d+1)/(r-1)}) by Lefmann [30]. Finally, we remark that a non-trivial upper bound of O⁡(nd⌊(k+2)/2⌋)O(n^{\frac{d}{\lfloor(k+2)/2\rfloor}}) on faff​(n,d,k,k+2)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,k,k+2) was obtained by Lefmann [30], and was subsequently improved to O⁡(nd2​⌊(k+2)/4⌋​(1−12​⌊(k+2)/4⌋​d+1))O(n^{\frac{d}{2\lfloor(k+2)/4\rfloor}(1-\frac{1}{2\lfloor(k+2)/4\rfloor d+1})}) by Suk and Zeng [40].

Brass and Knauer [8] also asked the following related problem: given n,d,k,r∈ℕn,d,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<dk<d and r⩾d+1r\geqslant d+1, what is the maximum number flin​(n,d,k,r)f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,r) of points from [n]d[n]^{d} such that any kk-dimensional linear subspace contains at most r−1r-1 of these points? For k=1k=1, this number is (up to a constant) equal to the number of primitive lattice points in [n]d[n]^{d}, which is well known to be Θ⁡(nd)\Theta(n^{d}). In general, Balko et al. [3] showed that flin​(n,d,k,r)=O⁡(nd⁡(d−k)/(d−1))f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,r)=O(n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)}). For k=d−1k=d-1, Bárány et al. [5] proved that flin​(n,d,d−1,r)=Θ⁡(nd/(d−1))f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,d-1,r)=\Theta(n^{d/(d-1)}). Brass and Knauer [8, Conjecture 9] conjectured that flin​(n,d,k,k+1)=Θ⁡(nd⁡(d−k)/(d−1))f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,k+1)=\Theta(n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)}). However, Lefmann [31] refuted their conjecture for most values of kk and dd by showing that flin​(n,d,k,k+1)=O⁡(nd/⌈k/2⌉)f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,k+1)=O(n^{d/\lceil k/2\rceil}). More recently, Sudakov and Tomon [38, Theorem 1.5] showed that flin​(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(nd⁡(d−k)/(d−1))f_{\text{lin}}(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)}) for r>dkr>d^{k}. We will prove the following theorem, which recovers the result of Bárány et al. [5] and extends the result of Sudakov and Tomon [38] to a larger regime for rr, but only up to polylog factors.

Theorem 1.2.

Let d,k,r∈ℕd,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<dk<d and r⩾k+1r\geqslant k+1. Then flin​(n,d,k,r)=Ω⁡(gd,k,r​(n))f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,r)=\Omega(g_{d,k,r}(n)), where

gd,k,r​(n)={nd⁡(r−k)/(r−1), if ​r<d,nd⁡(d−k)/(d−1)/(log⁡n)1/(d−1), otherwise.g_{d,k,r}(n)=\begin{cases}n^{d(r-k)/(r-1)},&\text{ if }r<d,\\ n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)}/(\log n)^{1/(d-1)},&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

In particular, if r=k+1r=k+1, then flin​(n,d,k,k+1)=Ω⁡(hd,k​(n))f_{\mathrm{lin}}(n,d,k,k+1)=\Omega(h_{d,k}(n)), where

gd,k​(n)={nd⁡(d−k)/(d−1)/(log⁡n)1/(d−1), if ​k=d−1,nd/k, otherwise.g_{d,k}(n)=\begin{cases}n^{d(d-k)/(d-1)}/(\log n)^{1/(d-1)},&\text{ if }k=d-1,\\ n^{d/k},&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

Erdős and Purdy (see [23, F3]) asked the no-four-on-a-circle problem: What is the maximum number fcirc​(n)f_{\text{circ}}(n) of points that can be placed in an n×nn\times n integer grid so that no four points lie on a circle, where a line is also considered to be a degenerate circle? Guy [23] mentions that Erdős and Purdy proved fcirc​(n)=Ω⁡(n2/3−o⁡(1))f_{\text{circ}}(n)=\Omega(n^{2/3-o(1)}). Thiele [43] (see also [42]) subsequently improved this bound to fcirc​(n)>n/4f_{\text{circ}}(n)>n/4 by taking a suitable subset of a modular parabola. This matches (up to a constant) the obvious upper bound of 3​n3n obtained by partitioning [n]2[n]^{2} into nn vertical lines. By forbidding isosceles trapezia with a horizontal axis of symmetry, Thiele [42] proved fcirc​(n)<5​n/2f_{\text{circ}}(n)<5n/2. We improve on the lower bound of Thiele using a randomised construction. To do so, we determine the asymptotic count of concyclic quadruples in [n]2[n]^{2}, a quantity interesting in its own right.

Theorem 1.3.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, the number of cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2} is γ​n5+O⁡(n4+1829+ε)\gamma n^{5}+O(n^{4+\frac{18}{29}+\varepsilon}), where γ\gamma is as defined in (12).

Corollary 1.4.

Suppose nn is large enough. Then there are at least 7​n/127n/12 points in [n]2[n]^{2} such that no four are collinear or concyclic, that is, fcirc​(n)⩾7​n/12f_{\text{circ}}(n)\geqslant 7n/12.

The proof of Corollary 1.4 is computer-assisted. We use a computer program (see Lemma 4.5) to obtain a rigorous approximation of the constant γ\gamma appearing in Theorem 1.3, which implies a bound with a constant slightly larger than 7/127/12 in Corollary 1.4.

Thiele [42] asked the following high dimensional version of the no-four-on-a-circle problem in his thesis: What is the maximum number fsph​(n,d)f_{\text{sph}}(n,d) of points in [n]d[n]^{d} so that no d+2d+2 points lie on a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional sphere, where a hyperplane is also considered to be a degenerate sphere? Thiele proved an Ω⁡(n1/(d−1))\Omega(n^{1/(d-1)}) lower bound by considering a suitable subset of the modular moment curve. The same problem was also subsequently asked by Brass, Moser, and Pach in their monograph [9, Section 10.1, Problem 4]. Suk and White [39] recently improved Thiele’s bound to Ω⁡(n3/(d+1)−o⁡(1))\Omega(n^{3/(d+1)-o(1)}) for d⩾3d\geqslant 3 using a randomised construction. We prove the following bounds on the count S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) of (d+2)(d+2)-tuples of points in [n]d[n]^{d} that lie in a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional sphere.

Theorem 1.5.

There is a constant cc such that nd2+d−2≲S⁡(n,d)≲nd2+2​d−4+c/log⁡log⁡n+nd2+d​log⁡nn^{d^{2}+d-2}\lesssim S(n,d)\lesssim n^{d^{2}+2d-4+c/\log\log n}+n^{d^{2}+d}\log n for every integer d⩾3d\geqslant 3.

As a corollary, we obtain the following improvement to Suk and White’s result.

Corollary 1.6.

There is a constant cc such that fsph​(n,d)=Ω⁡(nmin⁡{d,4}d+1−clog⁡log⁡n)f_{\mathrm{sph}}(n,d)=\Omega\left(n^{\frac{\min\{d,4\}}{d+1}-\frac{c}{\log\log n}}\right) for all d⩾3d\geqslant 3.

Suk and White [39, Conjecture 1.2] conjectured that fsph​(n,d)=Ω⁡(nd/(d+1))f_{\text{sph}}(n,d)=\Omega(n^{d/(d+1)}) for d⩾3d\geqslant 3. Their results imply this bound for d=3d=3 up to a o⁡(1)o(1) term in the exponent. Similarly, Corollary 1.6 implies this bound for d=4d=4 up to a o⁡(1)o(1) term in the exponent.

Note the gap between lower and upper bounds in Theorem 1.5. We conjecture that the true order of growth of S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) is close to the lower bound – see Conjecture 5.1 and the related discussion in Section 5.1. Together with an estimate on the number of (d+2)(d+2)-tuples of points lying on hyperplanes in [n]d[n]^{d} (Proposition 1.8), this would imply fsph​(n)=Ω​(n)f_{\text{sph}}(n)=\Omega(n).

1.1. Random constructions for extremal lattice problems

Guy and Kelly [24] showed that the number of collinear triples of points in [n]2[n]^{2} is equal to Θ⁡(n4​log⁡n)\Theta(n^{4}\log n), which, by the deletion method, yields a set of size Ω⁡(n/log⁡n)\Omega(n/\sqrt{\log n}) with no three collinear points. This bound can be improved further to Ω⁡(n​log⁡log⁡n/log⁡n)\Omega(n\sqrt{\log\log n/\log n}) by using a result of Cooper and Mubayi [12] about the chromatic number of kk-uniform hypergraphs (see also [10]). While algebraic constructions of size Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) are known for the no-three-in-line problem, it is not known whether a randomised construction of this size exists. Green [20, Problem 72] raised the question whether any no-33-in-a-line-subset of large enough size reduces to an algebraic curve modulo some prime. A construction exhibiting some weak pseudorandomness properties could give a negative answer to Green’s question. See also Eppstein’s blog post [19] for a discussion of randomised constructions of no-three-in-line sets. For the related no-four-on-a-circle problem, Corollary 1.4 shows that random constructions of size Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) exist. This would also be true in higher dimensions if Conjecture 5.1 holds.

1.2. Methods

All the problems we consider involve determining the largest size of an independent set α⁡(ℋ)\alpha(\mathcal{H}) of some rr-uniform hypergraph ℋ\mathcal{H}, with vertices V⁡(ℋ)=[n]dV(\mathcal{H})=[n]^{d} and rr vertices forming an edge if and only if they lie on a circle, a sphere, an affine subspace or a linear subspace. The deletion method yields the following lower bound on α⁡(ℋ)\alpha(\mathcal{H}).

Lemma 1.7 (Spencer  [37]).

For any rr-uniform hypergraph ℋ\mathcal{H}, we have α⁡(ℋ)⩾r−1rrr−1​|V⁡(ℋ)|rr−1|E⁡(ℋ)|1r−1\alpha(\mathcal{H})\geqslant\frac{r-1}{r^{\frac{r}{r-1}}}\frac{|V(\mathcal{H})|^{\frac{r}{r-1}}}{|E(\mathcal{H})|^{\frac{1}{r-1}}}.

To prove each of our extremal results, we will solve the corresponding counting problem, that is, count the number of edges in the associated hypergraph, and then use the above lemma.

1.2.1. Counting cyclic quadrilaterals

The main ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.3 is Huxley and Konyagin’s [26] result that circles passing through four lattice points are rare among the circles that pass through three lattice points. Their proof proceeds via the unique factorisation of Gaussian integers. In particular, similar approaches are unlikely to succeed in higher dimensions.

1.2.2. Counting conspheric tuples

The main technical ingredient behind the proof of Theorem 1.5 is a result of Lund [32] that bounds the number of incidences between points and kk-dimensional affine spaces in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Specifically, we use the map Ψ⁡(x1,…,xd):=(x1,…,xd,x12+⋯+xd2)\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})\vcentcolon=(x_{1},\dots,x_{d},x_{1}^{2}+\dots+x_{d}^{2}) to lift (d−1)(d-1)-spheres to dd-dimensional affine spaces and then apply Lund’s result to the lifted point set.

1.2.3. Counting tuples with affine and linear degeneracies

Let A⁡(n,d,k,r)A(n,d,k,r) and L⁡(n,d,k,r)L(n,d,k,r) denote the number of rr-tuples of points in [n]d[n]^{d} that lie in kk-dimensional affine and linear subspaces, respectively. Note that L⁡(n,d,k,r)L(n,d,k,r) counts the number of d×rd\times r matrices with entries in [n][n] of rank at most kk. Katznelson [29] determined the asymptotic count of integral matrices of fixed rank as nn goes to infinity. As an almost immediate consequence, we obtain the correct order of growth for both A⁡(n,d,k,r)A(n,d,k,r) and L⁡(n,d,k,r)L(n,d,k,r).

Proposition 1.8.

Let d,k,r∈ℕd,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<dk<d and r⩾k+2r\geqslant k+2. Then A⁡(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(ad,k,r​(n))A(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(a_{d,k,r}(n)), where

(1) ad,k,r​(n)={nd+k⋅max⁡{(r−1),d}, if ​r−1≠d,nd⁡(k+1)​log⁡n, otherwise.a_{d,k,r}(n)=\begin{cases}n^{d+k\cdot\max\{(r-1),d\}},&\text{ if }r-1\neq d,\\ n^{d(k+1)}\log n,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

The special cases k=1k=1 and k=d−1k=d-1 of Proposition 1.8 have previously appeared in the literature in differing levels of generality. See for instance [4, Lemma 2] and [24] for k=1k=1, and [4, Proposition 4] and [39, Lemma 3.3] for k=d−1k=d-1.

Proposition 1.9.

Let d,k,r∈ℕd,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<min⁡{d,r}k<\min\{d,r\}. Then L⁡(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(ld,k,r​(n))L(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(l_{d,k,r}(n)), where

(2) ld,k,r​(n)={nk⋅max⁡{r,d}, if ​r≠d,nk​d​log⁡n, otherwise.l_{d,k,r}(n)=\begin{cases}n^{k\cdot\max\{r,d\}},&\text{ if }r\neq d,\\ n^{kd}\log n,&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

1.3. Organisation

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. We prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 in Section 2, Theorem 1.5 in Section 3, and Theorem 1.3 in Section 4. Finally, we discuss some open problems and directions for future research in Section 5.

Note.

It recently came to our knowledge that in an independent work, Dong and Xu [14] proved an n−o⁡(n)n-o(n) lower bound on fsph​(n,d)f_{\text{sph}}(n,d) for all d⩾2d\geqslant 2 using an algebraic construction. Corollary 1.4 gives a lower bound of the same order for d=2d=2 but with a worse constant. However, our construction is of independent interest since it is probabilistic – see the discussion on random constructions in Section 1.1. For d⩾3d\geqslant 3, Corollary 1.6 gives much weaker lower bounds than Dong and Xu’s Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) bound. Conjecturally, however, our random construction attains the Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) bound.

2. Avoiding affine and linear degeneracies

Let M⁡(n,d,k,r)M(n,d,k,r) denote the number of integral matrices A∈[−n,n]d×rA\in[-n,n]^{d\times r} of rank at most kk. The following theorem concerning the order of growth of M⁡(n,d,k,r)M(n,d,k,r) as n→∞n\to\infty is an immediate consequence of a result of Katznelson [29]. It follows from  [29, Theorem 1] by noting that matrices with rank exactly kk constitute the main term and that B⁡(0,n)⊆[−n,n]d×r⊆B⁡(0,n​d​r)B(0,n)\subseteq[-n,n]^{d\times r}\subseteq B(0,n\sqrt{dr}), where B⁡(𝐱,R)B(\mathbf{x},R) denotes the Euclidean ball of radius RR centered at 𝐱∈ℝd×r\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}.

Theorem 2.1 (Katznelson [29]).

Let d,k,r∈ℕd,k,r\in\mathbb{N} with k<min⁡{d,r}k<\min\{d,r\}. Then, M⁡(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(ld,k,r​(n))M(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(l_{d,k,r}(n)), where ld,k,rl_{d,k,r} is as defined in (2).

It is easy to see from the proof of [29, Theorem 1] that the above theorem also holds if we only allow the matrices to have entries in [n][n] instead of [−n,n]∩ℤ[-n,n]\cap\mathbb{Z}. With this observation in mind, we are ready to prove our results on counting tuples in linear and affine spaces.

Proof of Proposition 1.9.

The set of rr-tuples of points in [n]d[n]^{d} lying on kk-dimensional linear spaces is in bijective correspondence with the set of d×rd\times r matrices of rank at most kk with each entry in [n][n]. Then, the observation after Theorem 2.1 implies L⁡(n,d,k,r)=Θ⁡(ld,k,r​(n))L(n,d,k,r)=\Theta(l_{d,k,r}(n)). We remark that we do not need to use the observation for the upper bound; it follows from Theorem 2.1 itself. ∎

Proof of Proposition 1.8.

We have ndn^{d} choices for the first point in the tuple. Translating the space so that the chosen point becomes the new origin, the number of choices for the remaining r−1r-1 points in the tuple is bounded above by the number of (r−1)(r-1)-tuples of points in ([−n,n]∩ℤ)d([-n,n]\cap\mathbb{Z})^{d} lying on kk-dimensional linear spaces, which in turn equals M⁡(n,d,k,r−1)M(n,d,k,r-1). Then, recalling the definition of ad,k,r​(⋅)a_{d,k,r}(\cdot) from (1), Theorem 2.1 implies

A⁡(n,d,k,r)⩽nd⋅M⁡(n,d,k,r−1)=O⁡(ad,k,r​(n)).A(n,d,k,r)\leqslant n^{d}\cdot M(n,d,k,r-1)=O(a_{d,k,r}(n)).

The lower bound follows using Proposition 1.9 by choosing the first point from the box [⌊n/2⌋]d[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]^{d}, translating the space so that the chosen point becomes the new origin, and considering the (r−1)(r-1)-tuples of points in [⌊n/2⌋]d[\lfloor n/2\rfloor]^{d} lying on kk-dimensional linear spaces in the translated space. ∎

Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 follow from Propositions 1.8 and 1.9 immediately using Lemma 1.7. Note that, to prove Theorem 1.2 when r>dr>d, we use the counting result for r=dr=d as it yields a better lower bound on flin​(n,d,k,r)f_{\textup{lin}}(n,d,k,r).

3. Avoiding spherical degeneracies

Our primary goal in this section is to prove the upper bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) in Theorem 1.5, and consequently deduce Corollary 1.6 using it. We will also prove the claimed lower bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) in Theorem 1.5 at the end of the section.

3.1. Number of lattice points on spheres

In the following two lemmas, we prove an upper bound on the number of lattice points on ellipses and then use it to derive a bound on the number of lattice points on spheres. Although they are similar to Lemmas 3.2 and 3.3 in [36], we include their proofs for completeness.

Lemma 3.1.

There is a positive constant cc such that for any integer d⩾2d\geqslant 2, every ellipse in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} contains O⁡(nc/log⁡log​n)O(n^{c/\log\log n}) points from [n]d[n]^{d}.

Proof.

We will prove this by induction on dd. First, we consider the case d=2d=2. Let EE be an ellipse in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. We may assume that it contains at least 55 points from [n]2[n]^{2} because otherwise the result holds trivially. Suppose that EE is defined by the equation

(3) x2+b​x​y+c​y2+d​x+e​y+f=0, where ​b,c,d,e,f∈ℝ​ and ​c≠0.x^{2}+bxy+cy^{2}+dx+ey+f=0,\text{ where }b,c,d,e,f\in\mathbb{R}\text{ and }c\neq 0.

Plugging the five points into the above equation, we get a system of five linear equations in five variables with a unique solution. Since each of these points lies in [n]2[n]^{2}, the variables b,c,d,e,fb,c,d,e,f have rational values with the numerators and denominators (in the reduced form) equal in absolute value to O⁡(nα)O(n^{\alpha}), for some constant α>0\alpha>0. Multiplying (3) by the least common multiple of the denominators of b,c,d,e,fb,c,d,e,f, we obtain

A​x2+B​x​y+C​y2+D​x+E​y+F=0,Ax^{2}+Bxy+Cy^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0,

where A,B,C,D,E,F∈ℤA,B,C,D,E,F\in\mathbb{Z} with their absolute values equal to O⁡(n5​α)O(n^{5\alpha}). Now the above equation can be rewritten as

A​X2+B​X​Y+C​Y2=F′,AX^{2}+BXY+CY^{2}=F^{\prime},

for some F′∈ℤF^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}, where X=Δ​x+B​E−2​C​DX=\Delta x+BE-2CD, Y=Δ​y+B​D−2​A​EY=\Delta y+BD-2AE, and Δ=B2−4​A​C\Delta=B^{2}-4AC is the discriminant. Finally, note that the number of integer points on the above ellipse is O⁡(𝐝⁡(Δ))O(\mathbf{d}(\Delta)); see [27, Equation 11.9] for a precise formula. Here, 𝐝⁡(Δ)\mathbf{d}(\Delta) denotes the number of divisors of Δ\Delta, and is O⁡(nc/log⁡log​n)O(n^{c/\log\log n}) for some positive constant cc, by the divisor bound [25, Theorem 317].

Now suppose d⩾3d\geqslant 3. Let EE be an ellipse in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Further, let AA be the 22-dimensional affine subspace spanned by EE and let WW be the 22-dimensional linear subspace obtained by translating AA so that it contains the origin. Then there exists i∈[d]i\in[d] such that the standard basis vector 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} is not contained in WW. Consider the projection map πi\pi_{i} that projects points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} onto the hyperplane PP defined by xi=0x_{i}=0. Then the projection πi​(E)\pi_{i}(E) of EE is an ellipse. Moreover, the number of points from [n]d[n]^{d} that lie on EE is bounded above by the number of points on πi​(E)\pi_{i}(E) that lie on πi​([n]d)\pi_{i}([n]^{d}). Identifying the hyperplane PP with ℝd−1\mathbb{R}^{d-1}, the result follows from the induction assumption. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

There is a positive constant cc such that for any integers d⩾2d\geqslant 2 and 1⩽k⩽d−11\leqslant k\leqslant d-1, every kk-sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} contains O⁡(nk−1+c/log⁡log​n)O(n^{k-1+c/\log\log n}) points from [n]d[n]^{d}.

Proof.

We will prove this by induction on kk. For k=1k=1, the result follows directly from Lemma 3.1. Now suppose 2⩽k⩽d−12\leqslant k\leqslant d-1 and let SS be a kk-sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let i∈[d]i\in[d] be such that the standard basis vector 𝐞i\mathbf{e}_{i} is not orthogonal to the affine space AA spanned by SS. Such a vector exists since AA has dimension at least 33. Now consider the slices of SS obtained by intersecting with the hyperplanes HjH_{j} defined by xi=jx_{i}=j for j∈[n]j\in[n]. Each of these slices is either empty, a singleton, or a (k−1)(k-1)-sphere, and therefore contains O⁡(nk−2+c/log⁡log​n)O(n^{k-2+c/\log\log n}) points by the induction assumption. Summing up over the nn slices, we conclude that SS contains O⁡(nk−1+c/log⁡log​n)O(n^{k-1+c/\log\log n}) points from [n]d[n]^{d}. ∎

3.2. An incidence result

Let d⩾2d\geqslant 2 and 1⩽k⩽d−11\leqslant k\leqslant d-1. Further, let α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). Suppose PP is a finite set of points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. A kk-dimensional affine space AA is said to be α\alpha-nondegenerate with respect to PP if P∩AP\cap A is nonempty and at most α​|P∩A|\alpha|P\cap A| points of PP lie on any (k−1)(k-1)-dimensional affine subspace of AA. Recall that a kk-flat refers to a kk-dimensional affine subspace. We are now ready to state the following bound on point flat incidences due to Lund [32, Theorem 4].

Lemma 3.3 (Lund [32]).

For each integer k⩾1k\geqslant 1, real α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1) and integer r>kr>k, the number of α\alpha-nondegenerate, rr-rich kk-flats is O⁡(nk+1​r−k−2+nk​r−k)O(n^{k+1}r^{-k-2}+n^{k}r^{-k}).

Similar to nondegenerate affine spaces, we say that a kk-sphere SS is α\alpha-nondegenerate with respect to PP if P∩SP\cap S is nonempty and at most α​|P∩S|\alpha|P\cap S| points of PP lie on any (k−1)(k-1)-sphere contained in SS. Now suppose PP is a finite set of points in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that PP is contained in some kk-sphere but not in any (k−1)(k-1)-sphere, where 1⩽k⩽d−11\leqslant k\leqslant d-1. Then such a kk-sphere SS is unique and we say that SS is the spherical span of PP, denoted by Spansph​(P)\text{Span}_{\text{sph}}(P). Moreover, we say that the spherical dimension of PP is equal to kk. We will need the following lemma, which asserts that for a nondegenerate kk-sphere SS, a constant proportion of (k+3)(k+3)-tuples in SS have spherical dimension kk.

Lemma 3.4.

Let d⩾2d\geqslant 2 and 1⩽k⩽d−11\leqslant k\leqslant d-1. Suppose SS is a kk-sphere in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that |S∩[n]d|=m|S\cap[n]^{d}|=m and SS is 12\frac{1}{2}-nondegenerate with respect to [n]d[n]^{d}. Then the number of (k+3)(k+3)-tuples in SS with spherical dimension kk is at least mk+3/2k+3m^{k+3}/2^{k+3}.

Proof.

We use the following procedure to construct many (k+3)(k+3)-tuples with spherical dimension kk. Let T=∅T=\emptyset. In each step, we choose a point from (S∩[n]d)∖Spansph​(T)(S\cap[n]^{d})\setminus\text{Span}_{\text{sph}}(T) and add it to TT. We continue this process until |T|=k+2|T|=k+2. Note that the tuple TT obtained after this procedure has spherical dimension kk. There are mm choices for the first point that is added to TT. Moreover, it follows from the nondegeneracy condition that there are at least m/2m/2 choices for the point being added to TT in each subsequent step. Finally, we add one more point to this tuple from (S∩[n]d)∖T(S\cap[n]^{d})\setminus T. The number of choices for this last point is m−(k+2)m-(k+2).

Now, the 12\frac{1}{2}-nondegeneracy of SS implies that m=|S∩[n]d|⩾2​(k+1)⩾4m=|S\cap[n]^{d}|\geqslant 2(k+1)\geqslant 4, which further implies

m−(k+2)=m−(k+1)−1⩾m−m2−m4=m4.m-(k+2)=m-(k+1)-1\geqslant m-\frac{m}{2}-\frac{m}{4}=\frac{m}{4}.

Multiplying the number of choices across all steps implies that the number of (k+3)(k+3)-tuples in S∩[n]dS\cap[n]^{d} with spherical dimension kk is at least mk+3/2k+3m^{k+3}/2^{k+3}. ∎

3.3. An upper bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d)

We are now ready to prove the claimed upper bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d).

Proof of Theorem 1.5 (Upper Bound).

Throughout the proof, we assume that nn is large enough and c>0c>0 is a constant for which Lemma 3.2 holds. Let P=[n]dP=[n]^{d}. Further, let 𝒮\mathcal{S} be the set of (d−1)(d-1)-spheres SS that contain at least d+1d+1 points from PP and S∩PS\cap P is not contained in any (d−2)(d-2)-sphere. We partition 𝒮\mathcal{S} into 𝒩\mathcal{N} and 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is the set of 12\frac{1}{2}-nondegenerate spheres in 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒟\mathcal{D} is the set of 12\frac{1}{2}-degenerate spheres in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Let Ψ:ℝd→ℝd+1\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d+1} be the lifting map defined by

Ψ⁡(x1,…,xd)=(x1,…,xd,x12+⋯+xd2).\Psi(x_{1},\dots,x_{d})=(x_{1},\dots,x_{d},x_{1}^{2}+\dots+x_{d}^{2}).

We apply the map Ψ\Psi to the point set PP as well as to the spheres in 𝒩\mathcal{N} to obtain Ψ⁡(P)\Psi(P) and Ψ⁡(𝒩)\Psi(\mathcal{N}), respectively. Let TT be the set of (d+2)(d+2)-tuples in [n]d[n]^{d} that lie on (d−1)(d-1)-spheres. We begin by bounding the first part. Let T′T^{\prime} be the set of tuples in TT that are not contained in any (d−2)(d-2)-sphere. Then Lemma 3.2 implies

(4) |T∖T′|≲(d2)​(nd)d​(nd−3+c/log⁡log​n)2=O⁡(nd⁡(d+2)−6+2​c/log⁡log⁡n),|T\setminus T^{\prime}|\lesssim\binom{d}{2}(n^{d})^{d}(n^{d-3+c/\log\log n})^{2}=O(n^{d(d+2)-6+2c/\log\log n}),

We now bound the second part, namely, we bound the number of tuples t∈T′t\in T^{\prime} such that the unique (d−1)(d-1)-sphere that tt determines is in 𝒩\mathcal{N}. ∑H∈Ψ⁡(𝒩)|H∩Ψ⁡(P)|d+2.\sum_{H\in\Psi(\mathcal{N})}|H\cap\Psi(P)|^{d+2}.

For each integer j⩾0j\geqslant 0, let ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} denote the set of dd-flats HH in Ψ⁡(𝒩)\Psi(\mathcal{N}) such that 2j⩽|H∩Ψ⁡(P)|<2j+12^{j}\leqslant|H\cap\Psi(P)|<2^{j+1}. |ℋj|≲|Ψ⁡(P)|d+1​(2j)−(d+2)+|Ψ⁡(P)|d​(2j)−d=nd⁡(d+1)​2−j⁡(d+2)+nd2​2−j​d.|\mathcal{H}_{j}|\lesssim|\Psi(P)|^{d+1}(2^{j})^{-(d+2)}+|\Psi(P)|^{d}(2^{j})^{-d}=n^{d(d+1)}2^{-j(d+2)}+n^{d^{2}}2^{-jd}.

Plugging the above estimate in (5), we obtain

|{t∈T′:Spansph​(t)∈𝒩}|\displaystyle|\{t\in T^{\prime}:\text{Span}_{\text{sph}}(t)\in\mathcal{N}\}| ≲∑j=⌊log2⁡(d+2)⌋⌊log2⁡(C​nd−2+c/log⁡log​n)⌋(nd⁡(d+1)​2−j⁡(d+2)+nd2​2−j​d)⋅2(j+1)​(d+2)\displaystyle\lesssim\sum_{j=\lfloor\log_{2}(d+2)\rfloor}^{\lfloor\log_{2}(Cn^{d-2+c/\log\log n})\rfloor}\left(n^{d(d+1)}2^{-j(d+2)}+n^{d^{2}}2^{-jd}\right)\cdot 2^{(j+1)(d+2)}

|{t∈T′:Spansph​(t)∈𝒟′}|\displaystyle|\{t\in T^{\prime}:\text{Span}_{\text{sph}}(t)\in\mathcal{D}^{\prime}\}| ≲|𝒟′|⋅(nd−4+c/log⁡log​n+1)\displaystyle\lesssim|\mathcal{D}^{\prime}|\cdot(n^{d-4+c/\log\log n}+1)
⩽nd⁡(d+1)​(nd−4+c/log⁡log​n+1)\displaystyle\leqslant n^{d(d+1)}(n^{d-4+c/\log\log n}+1)
(7) =O⁡(nd⁡(d+2)−4+c/log⁡log⁡n+nd⁡(d+1)).\displaystyle=O(n^{d(d+2)-4+c/\log\log n}+n^{d(d+1)}).

=O⁡(nd2​log⁡n+nd⁡(d+1)−6+2​c/log⁡log⁡n),\displaystyle=O(n^{d^{2}}\log n+n^{d(d+1)-6+2c/\log\log n}),

|T′|=O⁡(nd⁡(d+2)−4+2​c/log⁡log⁡n+nd⁡(d+1)​log⁡n).|T^{\prime}|=O(n^{d(d+2)-4+2c/\log\log n}+n^{d(d+1)}\log n).

Note that the number of (d+2)(d+2)-tuples of points that lie on a d−1d-1-dimensional hyperplane in [n]d[n]^{d} is O⁡(nd2+d−1)O(n^{d^{2}+d-1}) by Proposition 1.8. Corollary 1.6 now follows immediately from Theorem 1.5 and the above fact using Lemma 1.7.

3.4. A lower bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d)

Here, we present the proof of the claimed lower bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d).

Proof of Theorem 1.5 (Lower Bound).

Let d⩾3d\geqslant 3. Fix a centre x0∈[n]dx_{0}\in[n]^{d} with each coordinate between ⌊n/4⌋+1\lfloor n/4\rfloor+1 and ⌈3​n/4⌉\lceil 3n/4\rceil (both ends inclusive). 4. No-four-on-a-circle

In this section, we will estimate the number of concyclic and collinear tuples of points in [n]2[n]^{2}.

4.1. Counting collinear tuples

Guy and Kelly [24] determined the asymptotic count of collinear triples of points in [n]2[n]^{2}. For r>3r>3, we use a similar method to determine the asymptotic count of collinear rr-tuples of points in [n]2[n]^{2}. Recall that, by a tuple, we mean an ordered set.

Proposition 4.1.

Let r>3r>3 be an integer. Then

A⁡(n,2,1,r)=2​(r+3)r+1⋅ζ⁡(r−2)ζ⁡(r−1)⋅nr+1+O⁡(nr​log⁡n),A(n,2,1,r)=\frac{2(r+3)}{r+1}\cdot\frac{\zeta(r-2)}{\zeta(r-1)}\cdot n^{r+1}+O(n^{r}\log n),

2​n⋅r!⋅(nr)=2​nr+1+O⁡(nr).2n\cdot r!\cdot\binom{n}{r}=2n^{r+1}+O(n^{r}).

For c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z}, let ℓc\ell_{c} denote the line b​x−a​y=cbx-ay=c. Then the set of lines that intersect [0,m]2[0,m]^{2} is L:={ℓc:−a​m⩽c⩽b​m}L:=\{\ell_{c}:-am\leqslant c\leqslant bm\}. 4.2. Counting cyclic quadrilaterals

We will now estimate the number of cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2}. It turns out that almost all cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in the grid ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} are symmetric, that is, they are isosceles trapezia. Huxley and Konyagin [26] have demonstrated this in the following setting. Consider equivalence classes of cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and circumradius at most RR, under translation. They show that the number of such equivalence classes of asymmetric cyclic quadrilaterals is O⁡(R2+1829+ε)O(R^{2+\frac{18}{29}+\varepsilon}). In contrast, there are c​R3+O⁡(R2​log⁡(R))cR^{3}+O(R^{2}\log(R)) equivalence classes of isosceles trapezia, where c>0c>0 is an absolute constant.

A closer inspection of Huxley and Konyagin’s proof reveals that it implies a stronger result. Namely, there are O⁡(R2+1829+ε)O(R^{2+\frac{18}{29}+\varepsilon}) equivalence classes of asymmetric cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} and diameter at most O⁡(R)O(R). This holds because their proof only uses the O⁡(R)O(R) bound on the distances between the vertices of the asymmetric cyclic quadrilaterals being counted. Accounting for the O⁡(R2)O(R^{2}) possible translations, we obtain the following lemma.

Lemma 4.2.

For any set A⊂ℤ2A\subset\mathbb{Z}^{2} of diameter RR and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there are O⁡(R4+1829+ε)O(R^{4+\frac{18}{29}+\varepsilon}) asymmetric cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in AA.

The following lemma (see [21, Section 3.1]) will be useful for counting isosceles trapezia. We omit its proof since it is standard, although it follows quickly from the observation that there are O⁡(L+1)O(L+1) lattice points within distance O⁡(1)O(1) of any line segment of length LL.

Lemma 4.3.

Let PP be a convex polygon in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. Then the number of lattice points in PP is Area⁡(P)+O⁡(Perimeter⁡(P))+O⁡(1)\mathrm{Area}(P)+O(\mathrm{Perimeter}(P))+O(1). Moreover, the number of lattice points on ∂P\partial P is O⁡(Perimeter⁡(P))O(\mathrm{Perimeter}(P)).

We are now ready to count isosceles trapezia with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2}.

Lemma 4.4.

The number of isosceles trapezia with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2} is γ​n5+O⁡(n4​log⁡n)\gamma n^{5}+O(n^{4}\log n), where

The number of isosceles trapezia with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2} is equal to the number of isosceles trapezia with vertices in [2​m]02[2m]_{0}^{2} such that each vertex has both coordinates even. 2​f​(a,b)⋅m5+1a2⋅O⁡(m4).2f(a,b)\cdot m^{5}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}\cdot O(m^{4}).

Now summing over all possible values of aa and bb, we conclude that the number of isosceles trapezia with vertices in 2⋅[m]022\cdot[m]_{0}^{2} and their axis of symmetry having slope between 00 and 11 equals

∑a=22​m∑1⩽b<a:(a,b)=1\displaystyle\sum_{a=2}^{2m}\sum_{1\leqslant b<a:\;(a,b)=1} 3+(−1)a+b2​[f⁡(a,b)⋅m5+1a2⋅O⁡(m4)]\displaystyle\frac{3+(-1)^{a+b}}{2}\left[f(a,b)\cdot m^{5}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}\cdot O(m^{4})\right]
=∑a=22​m∑1⩽b<a:(a,b)=13+(−1)a+b2⋅f(a,b)⋅m5+∑a=22​mϕ⁡(a)a2⋅O(m4)\displaystyle=\sum_{a=2}^{2m}\sum_{1\leqslant b<a:\;(a,b)=1}\frac{3+(-1)^{a+b}}{2}\cdot f(a,b)\cdot m^{5}+\sum_{a=2}^{2m}\frac{\phi(a)}{a^{2}}\cdot O(m^{4})
=∑a=2∞∑1⩽b<a:(a,b)=13+(−1)a+b2⋅f(a,b)⋅n5+O(n4logn).\displaystyle=\sum_{a=2}^{\infty}\sum_{1\leqslant b<a:\;(a,b)=1}\frac{3+(-1)^{a+b}}{2}\cdot f(a,b)\cdot n^{5}+O(n^{4}\log n).

We multiply the above count by 44 to account for isosceles trapezia with their axis of symmetry having a slope less than 00 or greater than 11. Finally, we add the count of isosceles trapezia with their axis of symmetry parallel to x=0x=0, y=0y=0, or x±y=0x\pm y=0. In the resulting count, we have also counted degenerate isosceles trapezia, namely, trapezia A​B​C​DABCD, for which AA, BB, CC, and DD are collinear. Moreover, we have counted rectangles twice since they have two axes of symmetry. However, each of these counts is Θ⁡(n4​log⁡n)\Theta(n^{4}\log n). Subtracting these counts from the total count merges them with the error term, and we get the desired result. ∎

The sum appearing in the definition (12) of the constant γ\gamma in Lemma 4.4 can be broken down into several parts, some of which we can express in terms of common number theoretic constants. However, since we are unable to express the entire sum in terms of such constants, we obtain rigorous numerical bounds on this constant in the lemma below.

Lemma 4.5.

The constant γ\gamma in Lemma 4.4 lies in the interval (0.35974,0.36017)(0.35974,0.36017).

Proof.

For N⩾2N\geqslant 2, let sNs_{N} be the partial sum

∑a=2N∑1⩽b<a:(a,b)=12(3+(−1)a+b)f(a,b).\sum_{a=2}^{N}\sum_{1\leqslant b<a:\;(a,b)=1}2(3+(-1)^{a+b})f(a,b).

We compute sNs_{N} in Mathematica for N=5500N=5500 to an accuracy of ε=10−5\varepsilon=10^{-5} to obtain

|sN−s~N|⩽ε,\left|s_{N}-\widetilde{s}_{N}\right|\leqslant\varepsilon,

where s~N=0.09309\widetilde{s}_{N}=0.09309. Next, we bound the tail sum

0⩽γ−sN⩽8⋅∑a=N+1∞66​ϕ​(a)240​a3⩽2.2⋅∑a=N+1∞1a2⩽2.2N.0\leqslant\gamma-s_{N}\leqslant 8\cdot\sum_{a=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{66\phi(a)}{240a^{3}}\leqslant 2.2\cdot\sum_{a=N+1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{a^{2}}\leqslant\frac{2.2}{N}.

Combining the above estimates and using them in (12) yields

γ−415∈[s~N−ε,s~N+ε+2.2N].\gamma-\frac{4}{15}\in\left[\widetilde{s}_{N}-\varepsilon,\widetilde{s}_{N}+\varepsilon+\frac{2.2}{N}\right].

Plugging in the values of NN, s~N\widetilde{s}_{N}, and ε\varepsilon, and simplifying yields the desired result. ∎

Applying Lemma 4.2 to the point set A=[n]2A=[n]^{2} implies that there are O⁡(n4+1829+ε)O(n^{4+\frac{18}{29}+\varepsilon}) asymmetric cyclic quadrilaterals with vertices in [n]2[n]^{2}. Combining this with Lemma 4.4 yields Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Corollary 1.4.

By Proposition 4.1, the number of unordered collinear quadruples is 7​π2360​ζ​(3)⋅n5+O⁡(n4​log⁡(n))\frac{7\pi^{2}}{360\zeta(3)}\cdot n^{5}+O(n^{4}\log(n)). Combined with Theorem 1.3, we get that the number of edges in the hypergraph encoding collinear and concyclic quadruples in [n]2[n]^{2} is (γ+7​π2360​ζ​(3)+o⁡(1))​n5<c​n5(\gamma+\frac{7\pi^{2}}{360\zeta(3)}+o(1))n^{5}<cn^{5}, with c=0.51983c=0.51983, using Lemma 4.5. Finally, by Lemma 1.7, we have that fc​i​r​c​(n)⩾34​(14​c)13​n>712​nf_{circ}(n)\geqslant\frac{3}{4}(\frac{1}{4c})^{\frac{1}{3}}n>\frac{7}{12}n. ∎

5. Concluding remarks

To conclude, we highlight some open problems and potential directions for future research.

5.1. Improving bounds on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d)

As mentioned in the introduction, we conjecture that the following stronger upper bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) holds.

Conjecture 5.1.

For any integer d⩾2d\geqslant 2, we have S⁡(n,d)=O⁡(nd2+d−1)S(n,d)=O(n^{d^{2}+d-1}).

We have confirmed this conjecture for d=2d=2 in Theorem 1.3. For d⩾3d\geqslant 3, it is plausible that an even stronger bound holds, namely, S⁡(n,d)=nd2+d−2+o⁡(1)S(n,d)=n^{d^{2}+d-2+o(1)}. If true, this would imply that the lower bound in Theorem 1.5 is sharp up to a o⁡(1)o(1) term in the exponent. Exact computations of S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) for small values of nn and dd seem consistent with the above estimates.

Assuming joint spatial and modular equidistribution of lattice points on spheres of the form x12+⋯+xd2=mx_{1}^{2}+\dots+x_{d}^{2}=m, where m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, yields a heuristic for the stronger upper bound mentioned above. Here, spatial equidistribution refers to equidistribution with respect to the Lebesgue measure on the sphere, and modular equidistribution refers to equidistribution of mod kk residues of the lattice points on the sphere over the mod kk solutions to the equation defining the sphere, where k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. By joint equidistribution, we mean that modular equidistribution holds locally within small slices of the sphere. Spatial equidistribution of lattice points on spheres is known classically (see [27, Section 11.6]), but not in conjunction with modular equidistribution. We remark that this approach fails in two dimensions due to a special symmetry corresponding to isosceles trapezoids.

Finally, we also highlight a connection to random matrix theory. Let 𝐱(1),…,𝐱(d+2)\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(d+2)} be d+2d+2 points in [n]d[n]^{d}. If they lie on a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional sphere, then the matrix

A⁡(𝐱(1),…,𝐱(d+2))≔[1x1(1)…xd(1)‖𝐱(1)‖22⋱1x1(d+2)…x2(d+2)‖𝐱(d+2)‖22]A(\mathbf{x}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{x}^{(d+2)})\coloneqq\begin{bmatrix}1&x^{(1)}_{1}&\dots&x^{(1)}_{d}&\|\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\|_{2}^{2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 1&x^{(d+2)}_{1}&\dots&x^{(d+2)}_{2}&\|\mathbf{x}^{(d+2)}\|_{2}^{2}\end{bmatrix}

is singular. For i∈[d+2]i\in[d+2] and j∈[d]j\in[d], let Xj(i)X^{(i)}_{j} be iid random variables with distribution Uniform​([n])\text{Uniform}([n]). Then S⁡(n,d)S(n,d) is bounded above by

(14) ℙ⁡(det(A⁡(𝐗(1),…,𝐗(d+2)))=0)⋅nd⁡(d+2).\mathbb{P}(\det(A(\mathbf{X}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{X}^{(d+2)}))=0)\cdot n^{d(d+2)}.

For discrete random matrices with iid entries, the dominant contribution to the singularity probability is from the events that a row (or column) is zero or that two rows (or columns) are equal [28] (see also [41]). Similarly, it might be the case that this is also the dominant term in the singularity probability in (14), which would imply an O⁡(nd2+d)O(n^{d^{2}+d}) bound on S⁡(n,d)S(n,d). To prove Conjecture 5.1, one would need better estimates on the error term.

5.2. Extensible no-four-on-a-circle

The classical no-three-in-line problem seeks to maximize the number of points that may be selected from [n]2[n]^{2} while avoiding collinear triples of points. Erde asked whether one can select large subsets of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} that avoid collinear triples. Nagy, Nagy, and Woodroofe [33] showed that there exists such a set with Θ⁡(n/log1+ε⁡n)\Theta(n/\log^{1+\varepsilon}n) points in [n]2[n]^{2} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Considering a similar extensible version of the no-four-on-a-circle problem would be interesting.

5.3. No-three-in-line in [n]d[n]^{d}

Among the problems on avoiding affine degeneracies discussed previously, of special significance is the no-three-in-a-line problem in high dimension due to its connection with lower bounds on r3​(n)r_{3}(n), the size of the largest 33-AP-free subset of [n][n] – see Behrend’s [7] and Elkin’s construction [16]. As discussed in the introduction, we know that faff​(n,d,1,3)=Ω⁡(nd−2+2d+1)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,1,3)=\Omega(n^{d-2+\frac{2}{d+1}}), and this is the best one can do using a strictly convex surface. Any improvement to this lower bound would correspond to an improvement over Elkin’s lower bound on r3​(n)r_{3}(n). Elkin’s bound was improved recently by Elsholtz, Hunter, Proske, and Sauermann [18], but a good enough improvement to the lower bound faff​(n,d,1,3)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,1,3) might yield an even better bound on r3​(n)r_{3}(n). In any case, we think that determining the order of growth faff​(n,d,1,3)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,1,3) is interesting even in its own right. Note that we only have the trivial upper bound faff​(n,d,1,3)=O⁡(nd−1)f_{\text{aff}}(n,d,1,3)=O(n^{d-1}).
